title: Charcoal: Burning Wood Without Burning It
description: Why starving a fire of air leaves carbon, how charcoal burners worked, and why iron needed charcoal
tryIt: Break open a cold lump of lumpwood barbecue charcoal outdoors and look closely, with a magnifying glass if you have one, for the grain and growth rings of the wood it used to be.

concepts.title: How it works: wood without air
concepts.contentHtml:
It is your first autumn. The shelter holds, the water is safe and you are eating every day. Now you want things you cannot pick up off the ground: metal, glass, a cooking pot. Every one of them needs a fire far hotter and cleaner than your campfire, and that fire starts with a strange black fuel. The trick is to cook wood while refusing to let it burn.

Wood is mostly cellulose, lignin and water. Light it in open air and it burns away to ash. Shut most of the air out and something else happens. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's charcoal manual sets out the sequence: first the wood dries out at 100 °C or below, then it is heated to about 280 °C, and both steps are paid for by burning a little of the wood. Around 280 °C the dry wood begins to break down by itself into charcoal plus water vapour, methanol, acetic acid, tars and gases such as carbon monoxide. This is pyrolysis, and once it starts it gives out heat of its own. Left alone it peaks at about 400 °C, and the black, brittle solid left behind is charcoal.

Why go to the trouble? Charcoal reacts with oxygen at a glowing red heat to form carbon monoxide, which then burns with a blue flame, so it gives a fierce, compact heat with very little smoke. Better still for a metalworker, its carbon does chemistry as well as heating: it is the fixed carbon that reduces the iron oxides of the ore to metal. That is why charcoal was the source of heat for iron furnaces before the mass production of coal in the 1800s.

It took an army of people. Bonawe in Argyll, founded in 1753, is the most complete charcoal-fired ironworks in Britain. Around 600 of its workers were gualadairean, Gaelic-speaking charcoal burners who cut the wood, stacked it, fired it and spent the season living in turf or wooden huts in the woods.

concepts.title: In the field: reading a charcoal mound
concepts.contentHtml:
Do not try this on a whim: a burn smoulders for days and gives off poisonous gas. But it is a masterclass in steering a reaction with earth and patience, and every step has a reason. This is how a village burner did it, as the FAO's manual records.

  1. Level a platform. Clear, flatten and pack well-drained ground. On steep hillsides in Scotland the burners levelled flat stands and faced the downhill side with stones.
  2. Stack it tight. Lay a grid of small logs so gas can move underneath, then build the pile as dense as possible around a central pole. The pole comes out before lighting, leaving an opening down the middle.
  3. Seal it. Spread straw, leaves and coarse grass over the pile, then 10 to 20 cm of earth or sand. Very sticky clay is avoided because it cracks and shrinks as it dries and heats.
  4. Light it from the top. A shovel of burning wood and charcoal goes into the hole at the top, with a ring of small air inlets left open round the base.
  5. Read the smoke. Dense white smoke means the fire has taken hold; over a few days it turns bluish and finally becomes practically clear. Red heat showing at a vent means wood is burning, not charring, so that vent is closed at once.
  6. Shut it and wait. Every opening is sealed and the mound left to cool: two or three days for a small one. One tonne of charcoal from 4 tonnes of air-dry wood was good practice; 1 from 6 was more common.
Safety The gas from a charcoal burn has a high content of carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and has no colour or smell, and hot charcoal can reignite when a mound is opened. The same gas comes off a barbecue, so never use a barbecue or camping stove indoors or inside a tent. Headache, dizziness, feeling sick, weakness or confusion near a fire or stove can mean carbon monoxide poisoning: get into fresh air, and if someone is confused, struggling to breathe or unconscious, call the emergency services (999 in the UK).

concepts.title: Myth check: pure carbon and vanished forests
concepts.contentHtml:
Charcoal looks like the simplest stuff in the world: black, light and burnt. Two popular beliefs about it fall apart when you look at the evidence.

Myth Charcoal is pure carbon.
Reality It depends on how hot the burn ran. In the FAO's figures, charcoal finished at 300 °C is only 68% fixed carbon, at 500 °C about 86% and at 700 °C about 92%. The rest is ash from the wood, about 3 to 5%, plus tarry, volatile matter. Hotter is not simply better, because the hotter the burn, the less charcoal you get, while low-temperature charcoal is corrosive and smoky because of its acidic tars. Good commercial charcoal, at about 75% fixed carbon, needs a final temperature of around 500 °C.
Myth Charcoal burners stripped the forests bare, so ironmasters had no choice but to switch to coal.
Reality Managed woods grew back. Oak and hazel were coppiced: cut so that new poles sprout from the base, ready to cut again every 7 to 10 years. Bonawe kept firing on charcoal until the 1870s, and old coppiced woodland survives nearby at Glen Nant. When Abraham Darby I at Coalbrookdale turned to coke, made from coal, one study argues the prize was quality rather than shortage: coke iron could be cast into thin grey cooking pots in cheap cold moulds, which charcoal iron could not. Where wood was burned simply for its ash, though, forests really did fall, as the next lesson shows.

Wait, really? Sweden's charcoal iron industry was still making more than 80% of its charcoal in earth mounds in 1940. Its biggest mounds held 100 to 250 cubic metres of wood and ran a 24-day cycle: four days to load, six to carbonise, ten to cool and four to unload.

title: Ash, Fat and Soap
description: Lye from wood ash, how fat turns into soap, and why lye demands respect
tryIt: Rub a few drops of cooking oil into your palms, try to rinse it off with cold water alone, then wash with soap and feel how quickly the grease lets go.

concepts.title: How it works: from ash to soap
concepts.contentHtml:
Weeks of charcoal and cooking have left you filthy. Your hands are black, your shirt is stiff with smoke and grease, and cold water just smears it around, because grease and water refuse to mix. You need a go-between, and the raw materials are already in camp: the grey ash of last night's fire and the fat dripping off your supper.

Plant ash is full of alkali. Pour water through it and the water carries off dissolved potash (potassium carbonate) and soda (sodium carbonate): historically, soda was principally obtained by leaching the ashes of sea plants, and potash from the ashes of land plants. The strongly alkaline liquid that drips out is lye. Boil fat with lye and they react in saponification: each fat molecule, a triglyceride, is broken into its fatty acids, which the alkali turns into salts. Those salts are soap, and the leftover backbone of the fat is glycerol (glycerine). The French chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul put this chemistry into concrete terms in 1823.

A soap molecule has two ends that want different things. Its charged head is hydrophilic (water-loving); its long hydrocarbon tail is lipophilic (oil-loving). In water the tails huddle together into tiny balls called micelles, heads facing out. Add grease and it is drawn into the oily middle of the micelles, which stay spread through the water and rinse away, taking the dirt with them.

This is old knowledge. American colonists made soap by cooking down animal tallow and mixing it with a potash solution from the hardwood ashes of their winter fires, and the method had barely changed for centuries.

concepts.title: In the field: the ash hopper
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries soap was a household job done with ash, fat and a big pot. What follows is history, not a recipe: lye is caustic, and getting the balance wrong gives a soap that is harsh on skin. This is how a 19th-century laundress at Fort Scott, Kansas, worked, according to the US National Park Service.

  1. Save the ashes. Hardwood ash from the winter's fires was kept dry until it was needed.
  2. Build the hopper of wood. Lye is well known for being caustic, so the hopper was wooden, built in a V shape and filled with alternating layers of ash and straw.
  3. Let water do the work. Water poured in at the top seeped down through the ash, dissolving the alkali, and the lye was caught in a ceramic or glass jug at the bottom.
  4. Boil it with fat. The lye went into a kettle with grease or beef or mutton tallow and was boiled until it thickened; changing the boiling time gave a harder or softer soap.
  5. Mould and wait. The soap was poured into a wooden mould and left to harden for up to a week before being sliced into bars.
  6. Salt it out (the factory way). In the industrial kettle method, adding salt makes the soap rise to the top and the glycerine settle to the bottom, so the two can be separated.

The result cleaned well but, as the laundresses knew, lye soap was hard on the skin.

Safety This is history and chemistry, not a home recipe. Lye is corrosive. The US Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry warns that sodium hydroxide lye can cause severe burns in any tissue it touches, and very strong solutions can damage the eyes badly enough to blind. Dissolving solid lye in water also generates a great deal of heat. If lye gets on skin, flush it with water for at least 15 minutes; for eyes, at least 30 minutes. Call the emergency services (999 in the UK) for any chemical burn, and keep lye well away from children.

concepts.title: Myth check: Mount Sapo and Roman soap
concepts.contentHtml:
Soap's history is full of good stories. Some of them are even true.

Myth Soap was discovered at Mount Sapo near Rome, where rain washed fat from animal sacrifices and ash from the altar fires into the River Tiber, and the word soap comes from the mountain.
Reality That is a Roman legend, and soap is far older than Rome. Excavations of ancient Babylon uncovered cylinders with inscriptions for making soap around 2800 BCE, and Egyptian records from about 1500 BCE describe combining animal and vegetable oils with alkaline salts. Reference books disagree about the early dates, though: one says ancient writings suggest the Phoenicians knew soap by around 600 BCE, and another dates soap-making with potash and soda only from about 500 CE.
Myth Romans scrubbed up with soap at the baths.
Reality Soap was used widely throughout the Roman empire, but mainly as a medicine. According to the reference work How Products Are Made, soap is not mentioned as a cleanser until the second century CE.

Wait, really? The very first patent issued by the United States, signed by President George Washington on 31 July 1790, went to Samuel Hopkins for a process of making potash and pearl ash. Potash was big business: the American potash industry followed the woodsman's axe across the country, burning the forests cleared for farms, until a United States that had decimated its forests came to depend on mineral potash mined in Germany from 1861.

title: Burning Stone: Lime and Plaster
description: Limestone to quicklime and back again, gypsum plaster, and why slaking lime gets so hot
tryIt: Mix a little plaster of Paris from a craft shop with water in a disposable cup, pour it into a small mould and feel the cup warm up as it sets; never put your hands or any body part into setting plaster.

concepts.title: How it works: the lime cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Your hut walls are wattle and mud, and every rainstorm washes a little more of them away. You need something you can spread like butter that sets like rock. The answer, strangely, is rock: limestone or chalk, burned and then brought back to life with water.

Limestone and chalk are calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. Heat a lump strongly and carbon dioxide is driven out, leaving quicklime, calcium oxide (CaO); the escaping gas forces its way out and makes the lump crumble. Drip water on the cooled quicklime and it steams and crumbles further. It is slaking: combining with water to make slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, in a reaction so exothermic that in the Royal Society of Chemistry's classroom version some of the water turns to steam. Spread slaked lime on a wall and over the following weeks it takes carbon dioxide back out of the air and becomes calcium carbonate again, chemically the same as the original limestone. Builders call this the lime cycle.

Why does it get so hot? Burning limestone soaks up a great deal of energy to tear the carbon dioxide away, which is why plaster-makers in the ancient Near East had to heat it to 800 to 900 °C. Quicklime is chemically hungry: when it meets water it forms calcium hydroxide and hands a share of that stored energy back as heat.

People worked this out astonishingly early. A materials-science study of ancient plaster traces the invention of lime plaster back to at least the Geometric Kebaran, around 12,000 BCE, and its use in architecture to the Natufians of 10,300 to 8500 BCE. Lime plaster then grew into a real industry in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, a period named because people in the region did not yet make pots: they were burning stone before they were firing clay.

concepts.title: In the field: from rock to wall
concepts.contentHtml:
You will not be firing a lime kiln, and you should not: quicklime is dangerously caustic and a kiln is industrial heat. But old lime kilns survive in many places, like the great stone bank of kilns at Charlestown harbour in Fife, and knowing how lime was used explains why old walls still stand. Conservation guidance describes the sequence.

  1. Choose the stone. Fairly pure limestone gives non-hydraulic lime, which hardens only by carbonation. Limestone with reactive silica and aluminium impurities gives natural hydraulic lime, which also sets with water and has a harder set.
  2. Burn it. Quicklime is produced when limestone is heated in a kiln, driving off its carbon dioxide.
  3. Slake it. Quicklime is combined with water to make a putty stored in tubs, a bagged powder called hydrate, or a dry-slaked mix made in damp sand.
  4. Mix and spread. Lime putty was used historically for plastering inside, while mortar for masonry seems to have been made more cheaply by dry-slaking.
  5. Let it breathe. The mortar has to dry out slowly and carbonate properly, reacting with carbon dioxide from the air over a period of weeks.

Gypsum plaster is lime's quick, cool cousin. Gypsum is hydrated calcium sulfate, CaSO₄·2H₂O. Heated to only about 130 °C it gives up its chemically combined water and can be ground into a fine powder, plaster of Paris; add water and it sets within minutes, warming as it goes. Neolithic plaster-makers heated gypsum to 150 to 200 °C.

Safety Quicklime gives off heat when it meets water. The US workplace safety institute NIOSH lists it as an irritant to the eyes, skin and airways that can ulcerate the inside of the nose, and the first aid for eye contact is to irrigate immediately with water. Plaster of Paris is safer but not harmless. In 2007 a 16-year-old school pupil in Lincolnshire put her hands into a bucket of it to make a cast; it heated up and set around them, and she lost eight fingers. Large amounts can reach 60 °C. Never set plaster around any part of a body.

concepts.title: Myth check: mortar that dries, and Roman lumps
concepts.contentHtml:
Lime is the quiet hero of old buildings, and it is widely misunderstood.

Myth Lime mortar sets by drying out, like mud.
Reality Drying is only the start. Non-hydraulic lime hardens by a slow process of carbonation, reacting with carbon dioxide from the air over a period of weeks, while hydraulic limes and cements set by reacting with water in a matter of hours. Lime mortar needs air, and it lets masonry breathe and stay flexible. Cement, by contrast, has a chemical set that leaves a hard, impervious material which can damage soft stone and brickwork, which is why conservators repair old walls with lime.
Myth The little white lumps in Roman concrete are a sign of sloppy mixing.
Reality These lime clasts were long dismissed as poor quality control, but a 2023 study led by Admir Masic at MIT found evidence of hot mixing: using quicklime, not just slaked lime, so the mix heated itself. When a tiny crack reaches a clast, water dissolves calcium from it, and the solution recrystallises as calcium carbonate that fills the crack. In the team's tests, cracked hot-mixed samples healed within two weeks, while an identical sample made without quicklime never healed.

Wait, really? Lime also helped make iron. Bonawe furnace in Argyll shipped in limestone from the north of Ireland, alongside ore from Cumbria and charcoal from across Argyll, to remove impurities during smelting. That story belongs to the metal chapter.

title: Pottery: Mud Made Permanent
description: Clay minerals, why firing changes clay for good, the oldest pots and simple kilns
tryIt: Pinch a small pot from air-drying or garden clay and let it dry hard, then drop a chip of it and a chip of an old terracotta flowerpot into separate glasses of water overnight and see which one turns back into mud.

concepts.title: How it works: clay and fire
concepts.contentHtml:
You have been boiling water by dropping hot stones into a bark tray, and it is slow, sooty work. The bend in the stream has a bank of sticky grey clay. Shape it into a bowl, dry it in the sun, fill it with water, and it slumps back into mud. Fire it properly first, though, and it becomes something new that could outlast you by thousands of years.

Clay forms over millions of years as rain, made slightly acidic by dissolved carbon dioxide, weathers the feldspar minerals that make up around 60% of the Earth's crust. The important mineral in pottery is kaolinite: tiny plate-like particles built from sheets of silicon and aluminium oxides, stacked in layers held together by hydrogen bonds. In wet clay a thin film of water separates the layers, so they slide past each other when you push and stay put when you stop. That is plasticity. As clay dries the water escapes, the sheets move closer together and the clay shrinks by 5% or more.

Up to here everything can be undone: put a dried, unfired pot in water and it will disintegrate and can be returned into a workable state. Heat changes that. Once the clay reaches around 500 °C, hydroxyl groups on neighbouring sheets join up, releasing water and leaving stronger, shorter oxygen bridges between them. This is dehydroxylation, which X-ray studies place between about 425 and 675 °C. The kaolinite turns into disordered metakaolinite and can never again be reconstituted into workable clay.

Hotter still, pots mature. Earthenware is fired at 1000 to 1150 °C, stoneware and porcelain above 1200 °C, where the feldspar melts into a glass that binds needle-like crystals together.

concepts.title: In the field: bonfire to kiln
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of history, pots were fired without a kiln at all. Archaeologists at the Ness of Brodgar in Orkney, working out how Neolithic Grooved Ware was fired, say the generally accepted view is a shallow pit with a bonfire built on it. Here is the sequence, as history rather than a weekend project.

  1. Temper the clay. Potters mixed gritty material into the clay; the Roman potters of Highgate Wood, north of London, used grog in their early pots and sand in their later, wheel-thrown ones.
  2. Dry it completely. The free water must leave first, giving firm but fragile green ware.
  3. Fire it in a pit. Pots are bedded in a shallow pit and fuel heaped round and over them. Experimental firings in Orkney reached 600 to 900 °C, and the Ness team stress that the length of the firing matters at least as much as the temperature.
  4. Separate fire and pots. That is what makes a kiln. In a kiln the pot to be fired is kept separate from the burning fuel; in a bonfire the burning material surrounds the vessels.
  5. Let the heat rise. In the later Roman kilns at Highgate, an updraught type, the fire burned below a floor of clay fire-bars resting on a central pedestal, and the heat was drawn up through the stacked pots to a single flue at the top.
Safety Any firing is a fire you are responsible for: use a legal, cleared site, keep water ready and follow local fire rules. A bonfire firing reaches 600 to 900 °C, and pots and embers stay hot enough to burn badly long after the flames die, so let everything cool fully before touching it. Firing to earthenware temperatures is a job for a pottery studio with a proper kiln. For a burn, hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes, and call 999 (in the UK) for a burn that is large or deep.

concepts.title: Myth check: farmers' pots and sun-baked clay
concepts.contentHtml:
Pottery is an archaeologist's favourite material because it survives almost forever, and because it changed what people could cook. Its beginnings upend a tidy story.

Myth Pottery was invented by the first farmers, once people settled down.
Reality The oldest pots were made by Ice Age hunter-gatherers. Fragments from Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi, China, date back about 20,000 years. They were made by mobile foragers who hunted and gathered in the depths of the last Ice Age, and probably used them for cooking, at least 10,000 years before farming appeared in that part of the world. In Japan, food residues charred onto Incipient Jōmon pots from about 15,000 to 11,800 years ago come mostly from fish and other freshwater and marine food. The exact dates are still argued over: other researchers point out that some evidence could put the early Chinese pottery as late as the end of the Ice Age.
Myth Sun-dried clay is as good as fired pottery, just less work.
Reality Sun-dried clay never passes the point of no return. Fill an unfired pot with water and it slumps back into clay; only heating to around 500 °C changes the mineral for good. Even fired pots keep secrets. Earthenware still holds some water in its structure, which is why the RSC notes that an earthenware mug's handle gets hot in a microwave while a stoneware one stays cold.

Wait, really? Fired clay is older than any pot. A small figurine of a woman, dated to almost 30,000 years ago, is the earliest known object made of fired earth: people were baking clay figures thousands of years before anyone, as far as we know, made a cooking pot.

title: Glass: Sand, Soda and Lime
description: What glass is made of, how Bronze Age and Roman glassmakers worked, and why old windows do not sag
tryIt: Sprinkle a pinch of sand on dark paper and look at it through a magnifying glass, then compare the clear grains of quartz with a glass bead or a piece of sea glass: the same silica, with its atoms in order in one and jumbled in the other.

concepts.title: How it works: three ingredients
concepts.contentHtml:
Half buried in the shingle you find a nugget of sea glass, frosted and green. You have sand by the tonne, ash by the bucket and limestone in the cliffs. Could you make this from scratch? People did, with no idea of atoms, more than four thousand years ago.

Glass needs three jobs doing. The former builds the glass: silica, which for ancient glassmakers meant quartz sand. The flux lowers the melting point of the silica: soda, which the Romans took from natron, a natural salt from dry lake beds around Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, while others used the soda in the ash of sea plants. Glass made of silica and soda alone slowly dissolves in water, so it needs a stabiliser as well: lime. Ancient Roman glass is classed as soda-lime glass.

The Romans got their lime almost by accident. It came as crushed shell in the sand, and two areas noted for high-quality glass, the Belus river in Phoenicia and the Volturnus in Campania, had sand particularly rich in lime; according to the World History Encyclopedia, Roman glassmakers seem not to have fully understood why lime mattered. Iron in the sand tinted ordinary glass a pale blue-green, the common natural colour of untreated glass, until glassmakers learned to make it colourless by adding antimony or manganese.

Nature makes glass too. Obsidian, a volcanic glass, was used by Palaeolithic people as a cutting material long before anyone made glass on purpose.

concepts.title: In the field: from beads to blowpipes
concepts.contentHtml:
Glassmaking is furnace work, and it belongs in a studio with trained glassblowers. But the way the first glassmakers felt their way forward, over thousands of years, is a fine piece of archaeological detective work. Here is the sequence.

  1. Start from glazes. Glass was probably first made in Mesopotamia towards the end of the third millennium BCE, most likely growing out of the vitreous glazes and faience already used for beads, tiles and pottery.
  2. Make fake gems. Almost all early glass was opaque and brightly coloured, a substitute for precious stones. Beads were the commonest product, and they were worked cold, cut like stone.
  3. Shape it hot. Glass vessels appear in the late 16th century BCE, probably first in northern Mesopotamia, almost always made by core-forming. Working the glass while it was still hot was a major advance.
  4. Scale it up. In Egypt, under the pharaoh Amenhotep III in the first half of the 14th century BCE, glassmaking reached large-scale production in permanent factory installations.
  5. Blow it. In the 1st century BCE, in Syria and Palestine, glassmakers began blowing hot glass through a hollow iron rod 1 to 1.5 metres long. Blowing was faster and cheaper; by the 1st century CE, as Strabo noted, a glass vessel could be bought for a copper coin.
Safety Do not try to melt glass on a campfire or in a home oven: molten glass and glass furnaces are industrial heat, and broken glass cuts deeply. To try glassmaking, book a session at a studio with trained staff and proper protective kit. For a burn, hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes, and call 999 (in the UK) for a burn that is large or deep.

concepts.title: Myth check: flowing windows and Pliny's beach
concepts.contentHtml:
Glass is a solid you can see straight through, which seems to unsettle people. Two of the most repeated stories about it are wrong.

Myth Glass is really a very slow liquid, which is why medieval church windows are thicker at the bottom.
Reality In 1998 Edgar Dutra Zanotto calculated that cathedral glass would need a period well beyond the age of the universe to sag noticeably. In 2017 John Mauro's team found medieval glass flows much faster than earlier estimates suggested, yet it would still take billions of years to change its shape by mere nanometres. The thick bottoms come from how the glass was made: window glass was blown into a large globe and flattened into a disk, and whirling the disk thickened its edges. A glazier would sensibly fit the thick edge at the bottom.

The confusion comes from glass's atomic structure. In a crystal such as quartz, the atoms repeat in a regular pattern; in glass they never settle into a fixed crystal structure, so at the atomic scale it resembles a frozen liquid. Cooled below its glass transition temperature, though, it takes on the physical properties of a solid.

Myth Glass was discovered by accident when Phoenician merchants propped their cooking pots on blocks of the soda they were carrying and found glass in the ashes.
Reality That is Pliny the Elder's story, from the 1st century CE. The glass historian D. B. Harden called it credible neither from the archaeological nor from the technical standpoint: glass was known long before the Phoenicians were trading in the Mediterranean, and the tale probably grew from the fact that the sands of the Belus were widely used for glassmaking in Pliny's day.
